items.q: Your recommendations service hangs. Minutes later, checkout — which never calls recommendations — is also down. What's the most common mechanism?

options.t: Shared thread pools — waiting threads starve every endpoint
options.why: Right. Threads are finite. When all 200 are stuck waiting on one slow call, the server can't serve anything — including paths that never touch that dependency. This is exactly what bulkheads exist to prevent.

options.t: The network link between the services saturated under the extra traffic generated by the hung dependency
options.why: A hung dependency generates less network traffic, not more. The starvation travels through shared in-process resources — threads, connections, memory — not through bandwidth.

options.t: Checkout and recommendations share a database table
options.why: Possible in some designs, but the question says checkout never calls recommendations — the classic mechanism that needs no shared data at all is thread-pool exhaustion in the callers they share.

options.t: The load balancer routed all traffic to one server
options.why: That would be a routing bug, not a cascade. The signature of a cascade is that every server dies the same way at once — because they all share the same starved resource pattern.

items.q: Why is exponential backoff, by itself, not enough to stop a retry storm?

options.t: It's too slow to react to failures
options.why: Backoff reacts instantly — the first retry can come quickly. Speed isn't the flaw; synchronization is.

options.t: The failed clients stay synchronized — waves further apart, but still waves
options.why: Exactly. Everyone who failed at t=0 comes back at t=1, then t=3, then t=7 — a synchronized army attacking in pulses. Jitter (randomizing each delay) spreads the herd into a drizzle. 'Backoff' without 'jitter' is a half-answer.

options.t: The exponential delays eventually grow so large that most requests give up before ever retrying
options.why: Real implementations cap the maximum delay, so this isn't the issue. The problem isn't how long clients wait — it's that they all wait the same amount.

options.t: It only works for idempotent requests
options.why: Idempotency governs whether a retry is safe to attempt at all — a separate concern. Backoff's specific weakness is that identical deterministic delays keep the herd synchronized.

items.q: What is a retry budget?

options.t: The engineering time allocated to improving retry logic
options.why: Nice guess from the name, but no — it's a runtime mechanism, not a planning artifact.

options.t: The maximum number of retry attempts allowed for any individual request before it gives up
options.why: That's a per-request retry cap (e.g., 'max 3 attempts'). A budget is fleet-wide: even with per-request caps, a million failing requests each retrying 3 times is still a 4x storm. The budget caps the total.

options.t: A fleet-wide cap on retries as a fraction of total traffic, e.g. 10%
options.why: Right. When the dependency is healthy, the budget is untouched. When it breaks, amplification is capped at ~1.1x instead of 4x — excess failures return errors immediately instead of retrying. A token bucket implements it in a few lines.

options.t: The time window during which a failed request may be retried
options.why: Deadlines bound how long retrying makes sense, but that's timeout budgeting. A retry budget bounds volume: what percentage of your traffic is allowed to be retries.

items.q: A call to 'charge the customer's card' times out. Why is blindly retrying dangerous?

options.t: A timeout means the outcome is unknown — the charge may have gone through
options.why: Yes. Timeout ≠ failure; it means 'no answer.' The charge might have gone through after you stopped listening. Retrying a write safely requires idempotency (p2c02) — an idempotency key so the second attempt is recognized as a duplicate.

options.t: Retrying will make the payment provider slower
options.why: True but not the specific danger here. Extra load applies to retrying reads too — the unique danger of retrying non-idempotent writes is duplicated effects: double charges.

options.t: Payment APIs forbid retries in their terms of service
options.why: Payment APIs generally support retries — via idempotency keys (Stripe made this pattern famous). The danger is retrying without one, not retrying at all.

options.t: It isn't dangerous — a timeout means the request never reached the server, so nothing was charged
options.why: The dangerous misconception itself. A timeout can occur after the server received and processed the request but before the response arrived. You cannot distinguish these cases from the client side.

items.q: What does a circuit breaker's half-open state do?

options.t: Lets 50% of traffic through to share load fairly
options.why: The name misleads — it's not about a fraction of traffic. Half of a recovering dependency's normal load could easily re-kill it.

options.t: After a cool-off, admits a few trial calls — success closes it, failure reopens
options.why: Right. Half-open is the automatic recovery probe. It answers 'is the dependency healthy again?' with a handful of real requests instead of unleashing the full herd on a barely-recovered service.

options.t: Serves cached fallback responses to all callers while the dependency finishes recovering
options.why: That's the fallback, which runs while the breaker is open. Half-open is specifically the probing state that decides when to stop using the fallback.

options.t: Alerts an operator to manually reset the breaker
options.why: That's how your house's electrical breaker works — a human must flip it back. The software version resets itself, and half-open is the built-in electrician doing the safety check.

items.q: A well-configured circuit breaker trips when:

options.t: Any single request to the dependency fails
options.why: One failure is noise — networks drop packets constantly. Tripping on single failures would make the breaker flap open and shut all day on a healthy system.

options.t: Error rate or latency crosses a windowed threshold with minimum volume
options.why: Right — e.g., 'more than 50% failures across at least 20 requests in 10 seconds.' The minimum volume matters: 1 failure out of 2 requests is 50% error rate and means nothing. And tripping on latency, not just errors, catches the slow-but-alive dependency that eats threads.

options.t: The dependency's dedicated health-check endpoint starts returning an unhealthy status
options.why: Health checks help load balancers, but breakers deliberately use real request outcomes — a dependency can pass a trivial health check while failing or crawling on actual work.

options.t: CPU on the calling service exceeds 80%
options.why: That's a signal for load shedding at your own edge, not for a breaker. Breakers are per-dependency and watch the dependency's behavior, not your own utilization.

items.q: Why does this book call an unbounded queue 'a deferred outage'?

options.t: Unbounded queues eventually fragment the heap and slow the garbage collector until the process stalls
options.why: Memory is part of the story but not the core. Long before allocation issues, the queue has already destroyed your latency and turned your CPU into a zombie-work machine.

options.t: Under sustained overload, depth — and therefore latency — grows until the crash lands anyway
options.why: Right. Waiting time ≈ depth ÷ throughput, so a growing queue is growing latency. Past client-timeout depth, the server is 100% busy and 0% useful, and the crash comes later anyway. Bounding the queue converts 'crash for everyone later' into 'reject some now.'

options.t: Queues can only defer work, not process it
options.why: Queues never process anything — workers do — and that's fine. Bounded queues are excellent burst absorbers (p1c11). The pathology is specifically the missing bound under sustained overload.

options.t: Unbounded queues lose messages when the process restarts
options.why: Durability depends on whether the queue is persisted, not on whether it's bounded. An unbounded in-memory queue does lose everything on crash — the crash it caused — but the defining problem is unbounded growth.

items.q: Backpressure vs load shedding — the correct distinction:

options.t: Backpressure slows producers inside your boundary; shedding rejects at the edge
options.why: Right. Inside your walls you control both ends of every arrow, so 'slow down' is enforceable (bounded queues blocking producers, pull-based consumers, TCP flow control). The public won't slow down, so the edge converts pressure into cheap, priority-ordered rejections.

options.t: Backpressure is for reads, shedding is for writes
options.why: Both apply to both. The distinction is where they act (inside vs edge) and what they do (slow vs reject), not the operation type.

options.t: They're synonyms — two names for rejecting traffic under load
options.why: Backpressure doesn't reject — it slows producers so work isn't lost. Shedding rejects. A system needs both: pressure travels upstream until it hits the edge, and the edge turns it into 429s.

options.t: Shedding is the more graceful, user-visible form of backpressure — the same mechanism with a softer landing
options.why: Neither is more graceful — they're complementary placements. Shedding without backpressure protects the front door while the kitchen drowns; backpressure without shedding jams the front door shut.

items.q: The timeout rule that must hold at every hop of a call chain:

options.t: Every service uses the same timeout for consistency
options.why: Uniform timeouts guarantee violations: if everyone uses 1s, a callee can spend 1s while its caller gives up at 1s — plus retries push it far over. Timeouts must shrink as you go deeper.

options.t: Caller timeout > callee's (tries × per-try timeout) + backoff + own work
options.why: Right. If a callee can spend more time than its caller will wait, every slow request becomes zombie work — computed for a caller who already left — while the caller's retry doubles load on top. Walk the chain and check the inequality at each hop.

options.t: Callee timeout > caller timeout, so the callee never abandons work its caller is still waiting on
options.why: Backwards — this is precisely the bug. The callee outliving its caller means it burns capacity on answers nobody will receive. Deadlines must shrink downstream, not grow.

options.t: Timeouts should be set to 3x the average latency
options.why: Averages hide the tail — p99 can be 50x the mean. Derive timeouts from high percentiles (p99 plus margin), and even a perfect per-call timeout still needs the end-to-end nesting rule.

items.q: Postmortem finding: when the recommendations service hung, product pages died because all 200 server threads got stuck waiting on it. Which fix most directly prevents recurrence?

options.t: Raise the thread pool to 800 threads
options.why: Buys minutes, not safety — a hung dependency will consume 800 as surely as 200, with more memory pressure to boot. Capacity is not isolation.

options.t: A bulkhead: recommendations gets its own small pool, plus a breaker with a fallback
options.why: Right. With its own compartment, a hung recommendations service exhausts 20 threads and the other 180 keep serving product pages — pages render with the recommendations row empty. The breaker then converts those 20 slow failures into instant fallbacks. Isolation, not capacity, is the fix.

options.t: Add a second recommendations replica for failover
options.why: Redundancy helps when a replica dies cleanly. This incident was slowness, and slowness usually hits both replicas (shared store, shared bad deploy) — while your threads still hang waiting on whichever one they called.

options.t: Cache recommendations aggressively so the service gets called far less often in the first place
options.why: Reduces call volume on good days, but the cache-miss path still exists — and under a hang, misses pile up on the same shared thread pool. Caching is a fine companion to isolation, not a substitute.

items.q: The edge calls service A with a 1s timeout. A does ~100ms of work and calls B: per-try timeout 700ms, 2 tries. What actually happens when B has a slow day?

options.t: Nothing bad — 700ms is under the edge's 1000ms
options.why: Per-try, yes. But two tries plus A's work is up to 1500ms. Checking a single number instead of summing the attempts is exactly how this bug passes code review.

options.t: A can spend 1500ms against a 1000ms caller — zombie work, plus the edge's retry stacks on top
options.why: Right on both counts. A computes answers for a caller who left at 1s, and the edge's retry stacks a second copy of the request on top of the still-running first. Fix: shrink B to ~350ms per try or a single try, so A's worst case fits inside ~900ms.

options.t: B will time out A's requests before this becomes an issue
options.why: B has no idea what the edge's deadline is — that's the whole problem. Without deadline propagation, each layer only knows its own numbers, which is why the inequality must be checked by a human across hops.

options.t: The edge's timeout cancels A's in-flight work at the 1s mark, so nothing is wasted beyond that point
options.why: A common and costly assumption: the caller giving up does not stop the callee. A's request keeps executing to completion unless cancellation is explicitly propagated — which most HTTP stacks don't do by default.

items.q: You're configuring retries for calls from your API tier to an internal pricing service. Which policy is best?

options.t: 5 retries, fixed 1-second delay — predictable and quick to recover
options.why: Fixed delay = synchronized waves: everything that failed together re-attacks together every second, 6x amplification. 'Predictable' is exactly the property you don't want in retry timing.

options.t: 2 retries, exponential backoff, no jitter — the delays spread the load
options.why: Better volume, same synchronization flaw: the herd stays in lockstep, just with longer gaps between waves. Backoff without jitter is the classic half-answer.

options.t: 2 retries, full jitter, 10% retry budget, retries owned by this layer only
options.why: The full package: jitter desynchronizes the herd, the budget caps fleet-wide amplification at ~1.1x during real outages, and single-layer ownership prevents multiplicative retries across the stack. Note the correct option isn't 'more retries' — it's controlled retries.

options.t: 10 retries with full jitter — persistence maximizes the odds that each request eventually succeeds
options.why: Jitter helps, but 10 retries means 11x worst-case load and multi-second added latency for a user-facing call. If two well-spaced attempts both fail, the service is down — attempt #11 discovers nothing new. Persistence past that point is just load.

items.q: A bounded queue feeds workers that push 'user is online/offline' presence updates to a chat app. During a spike it fills. Best full-policy?

options.t: Drop the oldest entries
options.why: Right. A presence update from 30 seconds ago is worthless — it's been superseded by newer state. Drop-oldest keeps the queue full of the freshest updates, maximizing useful work. Real-time telemetry (presence, live locations, metrics) almost always wants drop-oldest; the old data's moment has passed.

options.t: Reject the newest entries
options.why: Reject-newest is right for user-facing request/response paths (fail fast to a waiting caller). For streaming state updates it's backwards: you'd preserve stale presence data and throw away current reality.

options.t: Block the producer until space frees up
options.why: Legitimate backpressure, but here the producer is the chat activity itself — blocking would slow message handling to protect a best-effort feature. Don't let a nice-to-have apply pressure to the core product.

options.t: Grow the queue — presence updates are small
options.why: Un-bounding the queue buys memory pain and a backlog of increasingly stale updates the workers must chew through after the spike — delaying fresh updates even longer. Small items don't change the math of growing staleness.

items.q: Flash-sale overload forces shedding at your e-commerce edge. Which traffic goes first?

options.t: Analytics beacons and speculative prefetch requests
options.why: Right — zero user-visible impact, and often a huge slice of traffic (analytics alone can be a third of requests). Priority shedding means dropping in order of business damage per rejected request: telemetry, then decorations, then degraded browsing — checkout and login are last, ideally never.

options.t: A flat 20% of all traffic, dropped uniformly at random across every endpoint
options.why: Uniform shedding drops checkouts at the same rate as analytics pings — turning a survivable spike into a measurable revenue incident. Random is what happens when you didn't write the priority list in advance.

options.t: The largest requests, to free the most capacity
options.why: Size is a poor proxy for value — an order submission may be 'heavier' than an analytics ping. Rank by business damage per rejection, not bytes or CPU per request.

options.t: Requests from users who aren't logged in
options.why: Tempting, but anonymous browsers during a flash sale are your buyers mid-funnel — many are one page from creating an account and checking out. Auth status is a weak proxy for value; request purpose is the real signal.

items.q: The breaker on your recommendations service just opened. What should the product page do?

options.t: Show an error banner: 'Some features are unavailable'
options.why: Honest but needlessly alarming — you've turned an invisible internal failure into visible product damage. Save the apology banners for features users actively invoked.

options.t: Serve a cached or generic recommendations row — or silently omit it
options.why: Right. This is the graceful-degradation menu doing its job: stale-but-plausible beats missing beats error. Most users never notice a day-old 'popular right now' row. The breaker decides when to degrade; the pre-designed fallback decides what degraded looks like.

options.t: Wait and retry until recommendations respond — the page should be complete
options.why: This re-creates the exact cascade the breaker exists to stop: threads held hostage for a decoration. No non-essential component should ever be allowed to slow the core page.

options.t: Return HTTP 500 — partial pages violate the API contract
options.why: Failing the entire page over a missing accessory inverts the priority order: you've let the least important component veto the most important content. Contracts should mark such fields optional precisely for this moment.

items.q: When your edge sheds a user's request, what should the user actually experience?

options.t: A fast, explicit 429 with a Retry-After hint the client honors with jitter
options.why: Right. Shedding is a designed experience: microseconds to reject, a clear signal, and a client that comes back politely (jittered!) rather than hammering. Fast honest failure preserves the user's patience and your capacity — and the client's respect for Retry-After prevents the shed traffic from becoming its own retry storm.

options.t: A spinner while the request waits for capacity
options.why: Queueing shed-worthy requests defeats the purpose — you're back to growing queues, growing latency, and zombie work. If you had capacity to eventually serve it, you wouldn't be shedding.

options.t: Nothing — shed silently so users don't lose confidence
options.why: Silent drops are the worst UX: the app appears broken in mysterious ways, and client code can't distinguish 'shed, retry shortly' from 'crashed, give up.' Explicit signals let clients respond intelligently.

options.t: A CAPTCHA challenge that filters bot traffic out before capacity is spent on real users
options.why: CAPTCHAs address abuse, not overload — and they add latency and friction for the legitimate users you're trying to protect. During capacity emergencies, cheap explicit rejection is the tool.

items.q: Your database replicas crashed under load. Each one that finishes recovery and rejoins immediately crashes again. What's happening, and what breaks the loop?

options.t: The replicas have a corrupted state; rebuild them from backup
options.why: If recovery completes and the node runs briefly, the state is fine — the timing of each death (immediately after rejoining) is the tell. It's the returning traffic, not the data.

options.t: A thundering herd re-kills each rejoining node — hold traffic away and re-admit in stages
options.why: Right — this is GitHub's November 2021 incident exactly: replicas 'recovered only to crash again due to load' until GitHub proactively held production traffic away from them. Recovery is itself an overload event; without shedding, the herd re-kills every node that stands up.

options.t: Add more replicas so the load spreads thinner
options.why: New replicas joining mid-storm get the same treatment — each absorbs a crushing share of pent-up demand as it arrives. GitHub promoted internal replicas during their incident and it wasn't sufficient; shedding was. Capacity added during a herd is fed to the herd.

options.t: Restart every replica simultaneously so the returning load is shared evenly from the same instant
options.why: Closer to the right instinct (synchronized capacity), but the accumulated backlog plus waiting retries still exceeds total capacity at the moment of return. You must reduce demand — shed, pause queues, hold retries — not just choreograph supply.

items.q: Which failure mode of a payment dependency is more dangerous to your system, and why?

options.t: Slow — it eats caller threads while error rates look fine, evading error-based defenses
options.why: Right. Dead dependencies fail fast: errors return instantly, error-rate breakers trip in seconds, threads are released. A slow-but-alive dependency holds threads hostage for full timeouts while error rates look fine — which is why breakers must trip on latency too, and why timeouts must be tight. Slow is the assassin; dead is just loud.

options.t: Dead (100% errors) — a total outage is strictly worse than a degraded-but-working dependency
options.why: Intuitive but backwards for your system's health. Total failure is loud, fast, and trips every defense immediately. Your fallbacks engage in seconds. It's the quiet slowness that drains thread pools while dashboards stay green.

options.t: They're equally dangerous — both trigger the same defenses
options.why: They don't. Error-rate breakers catch dead instantly but may never trip on slow-with-successes. Defenses tuned only for errors have a blind spot exactly where the danger is highest.

options.t: Slow, because slow responses corrupt data more often
options.why: Right answer, wrong mechanism. Slowness doesn't corrupt data — it starves resources. The danger is threads held for seconds each while the dependency technically 'works.'

items.q: Interviewer: 'Solid design. What happens at 10x load?' Which answer earns the senior grade?

options.t: "The fanout workers saturate first — 10x puts them at ~3x capacity per my earlier numbers. Their queue is bounded at 60s of work, so beyond that the edge sheds: analytics and prefetch first, feed reads degrade to cached, posting stays up. Queue-depth alerts fire well before users notice."
options.why: A preloaded, ordered failure narrative: what saturates first (tied to earlier estimation), what the bound is, what sheds in what priority order, what stays sacred, and what pages the on-call. This is the answer the question exists to check for — composed before it was asked.

options.t: "Autoscaling will absorb it — that's what it's for."
options.why: Autoscaling takes minutes; spikes take seconds — and scaling amplifies downstream pressure onto the database, which doesn't autoscale. Naming a product instead of a failure sequence tells the interviewer you haven't watched one happen.

options.t: "I'd add circuit breakers around every dependency, load shedding at the gateway, backpressure between the internal services, and autoscaling on top — whatever spikes first, some layer of protection catches it and the system degrades gracefully."
options.why: The right vocabulary with no design: no thresholds, no priority order, no statement of what saturates first. Mechanism names without numbers and decisions read as a blog post, not an on-call rotation.

options.t: "10x is out of scope — we agreed on current-scale requirements earlier."
options.why: Scope-lawyering the most predictable senior probe in the interview. The 10x question isn't a requirements change — it's the test of whether you know where your own design breaks. That answer must exist regardless of scope.

items.q: A teammate's design puts an unbounded queue in front of the order service 'so no order is ever rejected during spikes.' Your review comment?

options.t: Approve — never losing an order is the right instinct for revenue-critical flows
options.why: The instinct is right and the mechanism betrays it: during sustained overload the queue grows until every 'accepted' order waits minutes, customers assume failure and re-order (duplicates!), and the process eventually dies with the queue in memory — losing everything it promised to protect.

options.t: "Unbounded means users wait forever instead of being told no — bound it at roughly capacity × client-timeout, reject beyond that, and if we accept an order, confirm it from a durable queue so 'accepted' actually means something."
options.why: Commits to the bound with a formula, names the failure the unbounded version hides (latency growth into mass abandonment), and preserves the teammate's real goal — no silently lost orders — via durable acceptance. Critique plus a better path to the same goal is the senior review pattern.

options.t: Suggest replacing the queue with Kafka — a durable, replicated log keeps every order safe through any spike, consumers drain the backlog at their own pace, and nothing is ever rejected or lost
options.why: Kafka's durability is real, but this dodges the actual issue: a synchronous user is waiting. If arrival exceeds capacity, consumers lag and the user's wait grows regardless of how durable the backlog is. Technology substitution isn't the fix; admission control is.

options.t: Request they double the worker count so the queue never fills
options.why: Sizing for the spike means idle fleet the other 99% of the time — and the next bigger spike refills the queue anyway. Capacity planning and overload protection are different problems; a design needs an answer for 'demand exceeds whatever capacity we bought.'

items.q: Two candidates address resilience. A: "I'd wrap all service calls in circuit breakers and add rate limiting at the gateway." B: "Payments gets a breaker — 50% errors or p99 over 1s across 10s trips it — falling back to queue-and-confirm; it also gets its own connection pool so checkout being sick can't starve browsing. Search gets no breaker: it has a cheap degraded mode, so tight timeouts and a partial-results fallback are enough." Who reads senior, and why?

options.t: B — thresholds, named fallbacks, and a reasoned decision to skip the pattern where it isn't needed
options.why: B shows the mechanism internalized: numbers, per-dependency reasoning, and — the strongest tell — a place where the pattern was consciously skipped with justification. Knowing where a tool doesn't belong is rarer and more senior than applying it everywhere.

options.t: A — uniform protection everywhere is more robust than selective protection
options.why: 'Everywhere' with no thresholds or fallbacks isn't protection, it's vocabulary. Undefined breakers misfire — flapping on noise or never tripping — and a breaker with no designed fallback just converts slow failure into fast failure with no plan for what to serve.

options.t: B, but their search decision is a mistake — every dependency deserves a breaker
options.why: Reflexive uniformity is exactly what B correctly avoided. Where tight timeouts plus a cheap degraded response already bound the damage, a breaker adds tuning surface and flapping risk for little gain. Patterns are tools, not tithes.

options.t: Neither — resilience machinery is premature optimization until load testing has revealed where the actual weak points are
options.why: Load tests rehearse the traffic you predicted; outages are the traffic you didn't. Basic overload protection is like error handling — a launch requirement, not an optimization to earn later. And the interview explicitly grades whether it's volunteered.

items.q: Postmortem: a 40-second network blip caused a 4-hour outage. Evidence: after the network healed, every service sat at max load for hours; the backend saw 12x user traffic. The senior root-cause and fix?

options.t: Root cause: the network blip. Fix: redundant network paths so blips can't happen
options.why: The blip was the trigger, not the cause — 40 seconds of fault cannot explain 4 hours of outage. Chasing trigger elimination misses the amplifier, and the next trigger (deploy, GC pause, failover) meets the same amplifier.

options.t: The blip was the trigger; unguarded retries were the amplifier. Fix: jittered backoff, retry budgets, edge admission control
options.why: This is the DynamoDB 2015 shape: brief fault, hours-long self-sustaining retry storm, resolved only when engineers paused traffic to let the system breathe. The 12x-vs-1x traffic delta is the smoking gun. Senior postmortems separate trigger from amplifier and fix the amplifier.

options.t: Root cause: insufficient capacity. Fix: provision enough steady-state headroom that a 12x surge like the one observed fits without saturating any service
options.why: Buying 12x steady-state capacity to absorb your own retry amplification is paying for the disease instead of curing it — and with unguarded retries, a bigger fault produces 20x. The amplification is unbounded; your budget is not.

options.t: Root cause: services lacked health checks to remove sick instances quickly
options.why: Instances weren't sick — they were overloaded by synchronized retries. Health-check removal during a load storm makes it worse: every removed instance concentrates the storm on the survivors, the GitHub-replica death spiral in miniature.

items.q: Your product-catalog database is degraded. You can serve 10-minute-old cached data or errors. The senior call?

options.t: Serve stale everywhere — availability beats freshness in a crisis
options.why: Almost — but 'everywhere' is the trap. Stale is safe where it informs (browsing) and dangerous where it transacts: charging a customer a 10-minute-old price after a price drop, or overselling inventory that's actually gone, creates real harm that outlives the outage.

options.t: Stale for browsing; checkout re-validates price and stock — or queues the order rather than charging on stale reads
options.why: The senior move is a split verdict: staleness mapped to consequence, not applied globally. Browsing on stale data is invisible; transacting on stale data is a correctness bug with a customer attached. And the degraded checkout keeps its promise-shape: accept durably, confirm when truth is available.

options.t: Serve errors — showing users wrong prices destroys trust
options.why: This takes the checkout-only concern and lets it veto the whole product. A 10-minute-old catalog page is indistinguishable from a fresh one for browsing users; erroring the entire funnel to protect transaction accuracy on the last step overprotects by a mile.

options.t: Serve stale everywhere, with a site-wide banner disclosing that prices and stock information may be a few minutes out of date while systems recover
options.why: The banner alarms a million browsers to protect the few hundred at checkout — and legally/practically doesn't fix charging someone a wrong price. Disclosure is not a substitute for re-validating at the moment of transaction.

items.q: You inherit a service whose HTTP clients have no timeouts configured (library default: effectively infinite). The backlog also wants autoscaling, breakers, and better dashboards. What ships first, and why?

options.t: Timeouts — nothing else in the resilience stack functions without them
options.why: Right. Infinite timeouts mean one slow dependency parks threads forever: breakers that trip on 'failures' never see one (the calls never finish), autoscaling spawns instances that hang the same way, and dashboards show green while threads drain. Timeouts are the foundation the other layers stand on — and the cheapest fix on the list.

options.t: Dashboards first — you can't fix what you can't see
options.why: Usually sound advice, but you've already seen the critical fact: infinite timeouts. Observability tells you where fires are; this is a known fire with a one-line-per-client fix. Measure-first is a heuristic, not a ritual.

options.t: Breakers first — they protect against the dependency failures timeouts merely detect
options.why: Breakers need failure signals to count, and hung calls with infinite timeouts never produce one — the call just never returns. A breaker on top of timeout-less clients is a smoke detector in a room with no air.

options.t: Autoscaling first — capacity headroom buys time for the rest
options.why: Against thread-parking slowness, new instances hang exactly like old ones — you're feeding servers to the leak while paying for them. Autoscaling addresses load growth, not resource capture by a hung dependency.

items.q: Where do you implement priority load shedding for an overloaded API, and what triggers it?

options.t: At the gateway, before any expensive work — triggered by a saturation signal, shedding lowest priority first
options.why: Right. Shedding pays off only if rejection is far cheaper than service — microseconds at the edge versus milliseconds deep in the stack. Utilization-based admission (in-flight requests, queue depth) tracks real saturation better than request rate, and the pre-written priority order decides who gets the 429s. Commit to the placement and the trigger; that's the whole design.

options.t: Inside each service, after auth and session loading, so shedding decisions can draw on full user context and history
options.why: By the time you've done auth, session, and context loading, you've spent most of the request's cost — shedding now saves scraps. Priority can ride on cheap signals available at the edge: route, header, API key class. Rich context is not worth the price of admission.

options.t: At the client — ship an SDK that self-throttles when it detects server stress
options.why: Client cooperation (honoring Retry-After, adaptive throttling) is a valuable layer, but it cannot be the mechanism: you don't control every client's version or behavior, and abusive traffic doesn't run your SDK. The edge must enforce; clients may assist.

options.t: Shedding is unnecessary if the rate limiter (p1c12) is configured correctly
options.why: Rate limits cap each client against a quota decided in advance; shedding defends total capacity against the sum of everyone — which can exceed capacity while every individual client is under its limit. Complementary tools: per-client fairness versus whole-system survival.
